utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. Today is Thursday, the 18th of February, 2010. I would like to first greet General Petkovic, our witness for today. I would like to greet the accused, as well as the Defence teams, and Mr. Scott and all his fellow OTP members. And I would also like to greet everyone in the courtroom. First of all, I would like to tell Mr. Kovacic, who asked the question as to whether or when I would put forward my dissenting opinion regarding the decision to admit evidence or exhibits. You know that quite a few exhibits were rejected by the majority of the Chamber, and therefore I would like to issue a dissenting opinion. Unfortunately, I did not have time to finish this opinion, because yesterday and the day before yesterday I was in this courtroom from 9.00 until 7.00 p.m., and I also had to prepare the questions that I will put to General Petkovic. Obviously, I will put forward my dissenting opinion next week, either Tuesday, Wednesday, or Thursday. But as the Trial Chamber said, the time you will have will be from the time you receive the translation, so there is really no urgency and you don't really need it within 24 hours, because you will have two weeks from the date at which you will receive the translation of this document. It seems that there is a typing mistake regarding my opinion on the document, but I haven't really looked at the number. But I will let you know what number it is. So this is what I wanted to say to Mr. Kovacic. Mr. Scott, I believe you wanted to take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may, Your Honour, I'd like to express my gratitude for the information you've just given me, and I hope you didn't take our request as in any way hurrying you. We just wanted to be sure that the document would appear. Of course, I know that you need time, so thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Scott, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President. Good afternoon, all of Your Honours. Good afternoon, Counsel, all those in and around the courtroom. Your Honour, there's one matter that the Prosecution thinks must be raised today and at the beginning of the session, before Ms. Alaburic completes her direct examination of Mr. Petkovic, and I want to preface my comments by saying as someone who's been a courtroom advocate for quite some years now, I'm not unsympathetic to the difficulty of the task involved. Having said that, and I don't think this is a concern unique necessarily to the Prosecution - the co-accused may share the concern and perhaps the Chamber will share the concern - given the constraints of time in the case, which are considerable and we've all dealt with, I think Ms. Alaburic dealt with some topics -- some central topics, if I can call them that way, very fundamental topics, in a very brief, some might even say cursory, fashion yesterday. Again, given the time-limits, the rush of time, that might be understandable to some extent. Let me give the Chamber three specific examples to make it less abstract and more specific. One was the topic -- actually, two topics, the April 1993 ultimatum, which everyone in the courtroom is well familiar with, and the events in Prozor at the end of October 1992. Those two topics were dealt with by Mr. Petkovic in a total -- a total of 18 lines -- 18 transcript lines of testimony. The question of the camps and detention, that topic and a very important aspect of that topic was dealt with in four lines of testimony, four lines of testimony. And let me give you a specific example on what that was. Here's the question. This is at page 49577-49578 of the transcript: "Q. In your conversation with the supreme commander of the HVO, did you mention the facilities of where these isolated Muslim HVO soldiers and able-bodied Muslim men could find accommodation?" Mr. Petkovic's answer, four lines: "A. Yes, he said that the HVO had facilities that can put up this number of men and that it was up to the army to disarm these men in the safest manner, and everybody else was somebody -- oh, sorry, everything else was for someone else to take care of." "Everything else was for someone else to take care of." Your Honour, that's a question that begs -- that goes to the heart of much of the case, and I suspect Mr. Petkovic must have a view -- a fuller view of what that means. And I suspect that both the Prosecution and the co-accused would like to know what that case is before their examinations begin. Certainly, someone was responsible. These camps were not run by themselves. That's just one example. Third example, Your Honour, was the questions of military discipline and justice. That was taken also very briefly. The Chamber may recall some sensitivity, I think someone described it yesterday, when a number of Defence counsel, the co-accused, were on their feet about leading questions, that this was a sensitive topic. It was again taken in a very brief manner. Now, what that leads me to, Your Honour, I wanted to give the Chamber some specific examples of what I'm talking about. But here's the concern, here's the concern: Ms. Alaburic several times in the last few days has raised that, Well, to the effect -- and I'm paraphrasing, so counsel, please, I'm not quoting, I'm paraphrasing, although I will refer to some parts of the transcript. Ms. Alaburic's position has been to the effect, largely, that, Well, if I don't deal with it now, I'll deal with it in redirect. And I'm afraid, Your Honours, that things simply don't work that way. Let me just refer to a couple of times. On Tuesday, page 49478, at line 11, Ms. Alaburic says: "And one more thing. We have established that 20 to 25 per cent of the time is used for follow-up questions to the questions of the Judges. That is why we decided not to put any follow-up questions during our examination-in-chief, but, rather, anything that we consider very important will be left for redirect examination." The second time on Tuesday at transcript page 49482, Ms. Alaburic, addressing Mr. Petkovic, said: "General, if you remember, yesterday we broke off while you were looking at a map of Mostar on the 30th of June, 1993. I'm not going to ask any questions about that map now. I'll do that in the redirect examination." Reference number 3, also on Tuesday, at page 49511 to 49512,

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: "I would like the topic raised by Judge Trechsel --" Excuse me: "The topic raised by Judge Trechsel is very important, and it's a comprehensive topic, and we will deal with it in the redirect." Then Mr. Coric at one point intervened, and expressing his concern about the number of important topics that it appears may be left to redirect, and on that point I must say that I share Mr. Coric's views. Following Mr. Coric's views, and I won't read his part of the transcript, but I think the Chamber will recall the several interventions that Mr. Coric made on the topic, Ms. Alaburic then responded to Mr. Coric and again made a reference to the fact -- and ended her comments -- or toward the end of her comments saying this: "However, if such topics as haven't been covered in the examination-in-chief, I preserve the right to deal with that in redirect." And as I said, Your Honour, unfortunately the trial process doesn't and can't work that way. You can't say a couple of words, take a topic or a subject in a very brief -- highly brief, highly limited manner, in the sense of putting your marker down, and then saying, I'll come back to it on a redirect examination, after all the other parties have had their turn. That's, unfortunately -- or otherwise, it just doesn't work that way. Your Honour, the Prosecution has thought about this overnight, and this came to our attention as we thought about it yesterday, as we reviewed the transcripts over the last two days last evening. There's really, I suppose, a couple of possibilities: either Ms. Alaburic has to be given some sort of reasonable time to address the topics in a full way so that all the parties, the Chamber, the parties, the Prosecution, the co-accused, could all go into their examinations with confidence that the topic has been fairly and fully dealt with, or, I suppose, Ms. Alaburic would have to give some kind of a commitment that she said as much as she can say and will not come back to it in redirect. I don't know that that's a workable solution. Or, number 3, following the redirect examination, as the Chamber has provided for in its guide-lines dated the 24th of April, 2008, the other scenario is the Chamber would have to provide -- would need to provide additional opportunity for the other parties then to have further examination following the redirect examination. The core position, Your Honour, is that, again, you can't raise topics very briefly on direct examination and, as I said, reserve the opportunity then to address them more fully once you get to redirect. That's the issue, and I lay it before the Chamber's attention, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, there are really two things which need to be carefully distinguished here. They are connected, but nevertheless need to be kept separately. The first is the question of redirect examination or re-examination, as I normally call it; same thing. It's quite clear that re-examination or redirect has to be on matters which arise out of cross-examination. That's absolutely implicit and understood in everything that Ms. Alaburic has said in every reference to re-examination, tested by the extreme case -- if there is no cross-examination, and we can't force anybody to cross-examine - they've just got the time and the opportunity to do it - if there's no cross-examination, there's no redirect examination. There can't be. So, of course it's implicit. Let's say we take our chances. We're not in court to gamble as Mr. Petkovic's advocates, but we are here to form judgements on his behalf, and to that extent we take our chances. If the matters are explored in cross-examination so that we can legitimately then go to them in redirect examination, then that's what we can do. If they are not raised or if, in redirect examination, we attempt to go outside the proper scope of that phase of the examination, then an objection to those questions would be legitimate and would be expected to be upheld, and that would be an end to the matter. And there really isn't any more to it than that. The other strand, which is where Mr. Scott started, is a different point, which is that we should have gone more into particular -- leave aside the redirect point. We should have gone more into particular topics in examination-in-chief. Well, Your Honours, with the greatest respect to Mr. Scott and the co-accused, the other Defences, what questions they ask in cross-examination is a decision for them. What questions we ask in examination-in-chief is a decision for us. And, actually, it would be no solution, anyway, for the Trial Chamber to say, at Mr. Scott's request, Petkovic Defence, you can have another hour, if we actually don't want to ask any questions during that hour. We'd say, Well, thank you very much, we've had that other hour, but actually those are the questions we want to ask, we'll see what the cross-examination is, and so far as we need or wish, on Mr. Petkovic's behalf, to re-examine based on that cross-examination, that's what we will do. And, Your Honour, the fundamental position is we didn't have to call Mr. Petkovic at all. Of course, we didn't have to call any witness. We didn't have to call Mr. Petkovic. When we do put Mr. Petkovic in the witness box, naturally he's exposed to cross-examination, but that's part and parcel of it. But what we ask him, then, in his evidence is up to us. If the Trial Chamber wishes to explore matters further, of course, you can always. Cross-examination within the legitimate bounds can be done by the parties having the right to cross-examine, and then we get on to redirect in exactly the way that I've described. So there is, in the end, nothing at all in this point. We should simply proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours, and good afternoon to everybody else. May I add another element, and I have, of course, discussed this with Mr. Nicholas Stewart. We decided that I should tell you about this portion. I consider that I don't need to convince anybody in this courtroom that the Trial Chamber is in charge of these proceedings and that they know full well what the rules are governing re-examination, and that the distinguished Trial Chamber has the right to interrupt any re-examination which is contrary to the rules of re-examination. I don't think that there's any reason not to believe Judge Antonetti -- not to believe that he is fully capable of conducting these proceedings according to the Rules and that he won't allow anybody in this courtroom to examine contrary to the Rules. So as far as I'm concerned, there's no possibility here of doing something in re-examination that they don't have the right to do, according to the Rules of this Tribunal and the guide-lines which the Trial Chamber has adopted. At this point in time, the question that arises is this, and it's going to be relevant to other Defence teams when they conduct their examination: What are the rights of a Defence team with respect to -- during direct with a respect to questions from the Bench, from Their Honours? If you remember, the Defence of General Milivoj Petkovic wanted the Trial Chamber to make a ruling so that they could see what the rights of other Defence teams are to react to the answers given in response to questions by the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel kindly slow down, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that practice in this courtroom has shown that the Judges can ask questions and do ask questions when they wish to do that, and to ask as many questions as they like, and we agree to that. That's not contentious. Now, the question is: What can be done with respect to the Judges' questions if Defence counsel conducting the examination feels that something has been left unsaid with respect to that question? And there are two possibilities open there: to ask follow-up questions in that regard and spend time that was intended for in chief, outside the plans drawn up for in-chief examination, without the desire of the accused, or the witnesses, or the Defence counsel that prepared the examination; and the alternative to this is not to enter into a debate about the topics raised by the Judges' questions, but to behave towards the Judges' questions as one would behave towards questions raised during the cross-examination in general. It is my opinion that each Defence team should have the right to respond and to add to the topics that were raised through the Judges' questions, that that is a legitimate right, and that they can clarify that in re-examination. But after that, all the other Defence teams also have the right to re-cross-examine if, in that way, the questions of the interests of their clients are raised. And in my opinion, that is the only logical solution and the only fair solution. And if we recall the ruling made by the Trial Chamber with respect to Judges' questions, which is a recognised right for other Defence teams to react and, thus, defend the interests of their clients, and if, through the Judges' questions and answers to those questions, in a way it affects the interests of one of the accused, then there's no dilemmas, as far as I'm concerned. Now, if the honourable Trial Chamber makes another ruling and says that in re-examination no Defence team has the right to go back to the Judges' questions and deal with them, then I would like to ask the Trial Chamber to make a ruling and decision whereby no Defence team, in its cross-examination -- does not have the right to refer to Judges' questions, and so the Judges' questions will remain as they were asked, as they stand. So this is obviously a subject that must be dealt with. And as far as I can say, it can be dealt with in any way -- any of these ways that I have put forward. The Defence of General Petkovic will, of course, respect any ruling made by the Trial Chamber. All I can say is that I regret having to talk about this 17 minutes before the close of the examination-in-chief of General Petkovic. Now, as regards the request made by Mr. Scott for additional time, this time we are absolutely opposed to that because, at the beginning of the examination-in-chief of General Petkovic, we decided about matters of time, we established the rules and regulations for these proceedings, and General Petkovic began his testimony under those conditions. And, therefore, I consider that those conditions must absolutely be upheld and cannot be changed during his examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may be heard just for a second. I try to stay out of these sorts of procedural issues whenever I can. Mr. Scott used one particular word that I thought was rather telling, and that was "confidence." That was the word, I believe, that he used. Whenever one goes into cross-examination, they have to have confidence that what they're about to cross-examine, the topics have been covered fully and fairly, and that what will follow from cross-examination, that is, redirect examination, will only be strictly for rebuttal purposes, that is, for anything that might have come up during the cross-examination purposes. Now, I understand the dilemma that everybody's having, and I think that the safest way to approach this -- the safest way to approach this is to simply allow all counsel to have re-cross-examination as a matter of practice. That way, by doing that - and we have that practice in the United States - this is to prevent counsel from, on direct examination, doing a little bit waiting for redirect in order to sort of what we call sandbag the other side. By allowing re-cross-examination, it then allows -- it forces the party who goes forward to actually put all their cards up front, and that avoids any last-minute, you know, need for re-cross-examination. In any event, I think all of us are concerned. Ms. Alaburic has a point. She has a lot of material to cover, little time. I don't share, I must say with all due candour, I don't share her viewpoint that the Judges' questions should be handled on redirect examination, because in doing that -- because unfortunately the questions coming from the Judges are coming contemporaneously with the direct examination. On the other hand, I do know that by dealing with them immediately, it takes up a lot of time, and I think the figure was 20 to 25 per cent, and I can -- from practice, I'm more than willing to accept that figure, if not higher than that. So there lies the problem. But I would prefer the practice be that everything be handled on direct examination, allowing the parties the possibility of re-cross-examination, and in this instance, because of the topics and because of who we have on the stand, to allow Ms. Alaburic the flexibility to do a thorough direct examination, thereby allowing the rest of us, who are concerned - and I'm not saying that I am one of them, but many of them, I know, are - to have a sense of confidence when we stand up to do our cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that everything has been said, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, in light of the comments, I would like to make an ever-so-brief response. Counsel -- both of Mr. Petkovic's counsel were on their feet, and I think I should at least have a chance to respond. Your Honour, I don't mind and certainly in fact expect that any argument or position put forward by the Prosecution or a concern raised will -- is subject, of course, to a fair and even tough response. However, I do not accept to have our position mis-characterised. I did not request at this point additional time, and the Chamber should not address, with all due respect, the issue that the Prosecution has raised before the Chamber in the context or postured by the Defence as Mr. Scott asking for more time. I have not asked for more time at this point. I have raised what the Prosecution believes is a very serious and good-faith concern. Now, having said that, Your Honours, I agree with Mr. Karnavas. This is not primarily about the Judges' questions. There's a factor of that. But, again, I don't want the issue -- the fundamental issue to be mis-characterised. This is not primarily about Judges' questions. This is about fairness in the examination process. And I still stand by -- again with some sympathy to Ms. Alaburic's position, I repeat again, you can't treat a matter in a very cursory fashion and then say, I'll come back to it in redirect. It fundamentally corrupts the process. Now, Mr. Stewart says, Well, they didn't have to put Mr. Petkovic on at all, on at all. Of course not, of course they didn't. But once they have -- but once they have, there has to be a fairness in the procedure to both the Prosecution and the co-accused. So that's our concern, Your Honour. The Prosecution felt that it was something that should be brought before the Chamber. We're, of course, as always, in the Chamber's hands. I do forecast, Your Honour, that some days from now -- some days from now we'll be having this very further discussion. I'll be happy to be shown wrong, but I forecast that we will. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since Judge Trechsel is not here today, the Trial Chamber will hand out its decision on the basis of what you have said and on the basis of what the parties have responded to the question at issue; namely, that you have realised that the Petkovic Defence did not address topics [indiscernible], in your view, are important topics; Prozor, for instance, the April 1993 ultimatum, and so on. I shall not go into details here. You feel that this is a problem, and you seize the Judges of this question. And you explain that this may have to do with the time factor. We will deliberate on the matter. I could tell you straight away what my position is, but out of respect for my colleague who is not here today, I shall not do this. On a personal note, and I would like this to be very clear, after Ms. Alaburic has completed her questions, I, myself, would put questions to General Petkovic, so we will be on the front-line then. I would like to say this. The Rules are very specific. There is an examination-in-chief, a cross-examination, and redirect. As far as redirect is concerned, the case law of this Tribunal, notably stemming from common law Judges, is extremely strict. Redirect must have to do with the cross-examination and ties into it very narrowly. The Defence controls its strategy entirely. If the Defence wishes to address a number of issues, it may. If it doesn't, then it doesn't. The best proof of this is the Haradinaj case, in which the Haradinaj Defence team did not wish to call any witnesses and stated that as far as it was concerned, the trial had come to an end. The Prosecutor did not get to his feet to say, No, he should conduct his examination-in-chief. The Defence is entirely free. If it wishes to do so, it can. If it doesn't want to, then it doesn't. The best proof of that is that if an accused wants to, he can testify. If he doesn't want to, he doesn't. That is what the Rules state. In addition, as far as the examination-in-chief is concerned, which addresses a number of issues, the cross-examination must, as far as I'm concerned, solely focus on those issues that have been addressed during the examination-in-chief. That is how this should be conducted, in this spirit. Even if the Trial Chamber is made up of Judges who come from civil law systems, it also has a number of assistants who know, as well as common law lawyers do, how the system works. We are working with American prosecutors, American attorneys, and only a few days ago an American attorney came to work with us in the Chamber. So this is familiar ground, as far as we are concerned, and we know how the common law system works. The only problem which I see at the moment, and I shall discuss it with my colleagues, whether we should force General Petkovic's team to address a number of issues and then provide additional time, but the Trial Chamber has set the time for all Defence teams. General Petkovic has 55 hours, and the Petkovic Defence was free to use this time as it wished. It decided to dedicate six hours to General Petkovic and to keep a little bit of time for Mr. Coric's witnesses, Mr. Coric's testimony, Mr. Pusic, and Mr. Pusic's testimony, if he is to testify. We don't know. Since the Praljak Defence has had its time, it kept a little bit of extra time in the event it wanted to put any questions during redirect. So all of these elements fit into one another. Of course, it hasn't escaped me that the Petkovic Defence did not address a number of issues. Nothing tells you that I might not put questions on these issues when I put questions to the witness. Why will I intervene immediately after the examination-in-chief? Things are not done haphazardly. I've been working for 30 years in a courtroom, and I know what a criminal trial is all about. I felt it was better to intervene then to enable all and everyone, namely, other counsel, during their cross-examination, if need be, to come back on things the witness has said when I put questions to the witness. This is a safety window. And then the Prosecution has everything at its disposal for the cross-examination of the witness. I'm also making sure that the Prosecution can work properly. I also make sure that the Petkovic Defence can work properly, because Ms. Alaburic, when she decides to conduct her redirect, can, if need be, revert back to my questions. No one is prejudiced in this way. This is what I believe. If I thought that were the case, then I would just remain silent, but that is not how I proceed, and certainly not in professional terms. The Trial Chamber will undoubtedly, either on Monday or Tuesday, state its position, a unanimous position, a decision taken by the majority; I don't know. Whatever the case may be, this issue will be the subject of an oral decision. Ms. Alaburic, I don't know how many minutes you have left. You have the floor to complete your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I start examining the witness, I would like to thank you for this explanation. For the most part, it jibes with what I wanted to tell my learned friend Mr. Scott. And my response is the following: We have spent the last two years analysing all the evidence called by the Prosecution, and we have analysed whether the Prosecution managed to prove the counts, the charges. And based on that, we decided that we didn't have to adduce any evidence to the contrary. Having decided that the Prosecution failed to prove some charges against General Petkovic, we decided not to address them in our case. After General Petkovic's examination-in-chief, we will have just one major topic that we want to examine him on, but unfortunately we won't have enough time to deal with it, and this is the labour done by detainees. Cutting my examination-in-chief short, down to 17 minutes that I have left, I decided to skip this topic, while making it clear to the Trial Chamber that I consider it to be very important, because I could see that His Honour Judge Antonetti wanted to address some documents signed by General Petkovic about labour by detainees, and I have no doubt this topic will be addressed in this courtroom. And if the Prosecution or my colleagues from the Defence -- other Defence teams want to address this topic, and I'm sure that Mr. Scott will want to do that, I will consider that to be a topic that has been covered in the examination-in-chief, and I will not oppose leading questions by my learned friend Mr. Scott, because we had to skip some topics or deal with them in the briefest possible terms because we consider them to be not in dispute when it comes to the innocence by the accused, General Petkovic. Now, I have some 17 or 16 minutes left, according to my calculation.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, we addressed the issue of your movements the past few days. That's document 4D2027. Your Honours, it's the separate document that I distributed to everybody two days ago. I assume that we have it on our screens now. Yes, we'll have it soon. Let me repeat the number, 4D2027. General, you have it in English only. Okay, now we have it in Croatian. Did you take part in drafting this document?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The numbers listed here, under the headings that indicate where you were, Geneva, Mostar, Sarajevo, what is the reference there? For instance, P12 -- 1038?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is the number of the exhibit admitted here at this trial where my name and whereabouts are mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, could you tell us, on the five pages of text that we have here, to the best of your recollection, is this an accurate representation of your movements relevant for the time-period of the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I have to make a correction. As regards November.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Please go ahead, General.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says that on the 8th of November, "Boban-Petkovic in Ploce." That's wrong, because it should read that Petkovic was in Split on the 8th.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can we please look at the last page of this document. That's page 5 in both languages. And then I would like to ask you, General, to correct this. And perhaps we can make it possible for the general to correct it on the screen. General, I think that you will now be able to cross out what is stated here for Ploce, and then you can just cross that out and write "Split."

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, now I would like you to initial this page.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And then we can go back to page 1, and you could perhaps initial page 1 as well, and then I would like us to get an IC number for it. If we could go back to page 1.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the document just initialled by the witness shall be given Exhibit IC01180. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, over the past few days we spoke at length about the obligations of the commander of a military unit. Now I would like you to give us some explanations as to the deputy commanders. Do deputy commanders have the right to discipline soldiers and officers in that unit?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The law stipulates that only the commander has that right, or if that person stands in for the commander for a lengthier time-period.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, could you please tell us, is the deputy commander part of the chain of command?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we look at the chain of command, in terms of individuals, only commanders, people designated as commanders are part of the chain of command, because you cannot have two people at the same place in the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, tell us, does the deputy commander have any inherent command powers?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The command powers must be defined and conferred upon him.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let me repeat the question. Does that mean that that person has or has not inherent command powers?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the organisational part of the command structure, he does have powers, and he is in charge of other services that are not in the strict operational or command sense.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, I don't think that the interpretation is correct. Could you please repeat your answer slowly? So I am asking you whether deputy commanders have inherent command powers.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He does not have any command powers when he's together with the commander. He has powers to carry out auxiliary, secondary activities in a command.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, when can deputy commanders have some command powers?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the point in time when the commander confers the command powers upon him and gives him the task and the time-frame for his actions.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If we go back to the topic of Stupni Do, and if we recall that Ivica Rajic sent his first report on the 8th of November, 1993, about the events in Stupni Do, and sent a supplemental report on the 15th, can you tell us whether you, as the deputy chief of the Main Staff, and the chief was Ante Roso, did you have any powers to take any measures against Ivica Rajic or any other HVO members?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was duty-bound, if General Ante Roso was not informed about that, to bring this report to his attention and to inform him about all actions that were taken. And in that case, he took it upon himself to act further.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Finally, General, I would like you to explain to us some of the statements that you made earlier. We've seen them in the documents that were admitted in this courtroom. 4D75, it's the penultimate document in the third binder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, let me get back to the disciplinary measures. That is not something I had contemplated as part of my questions, and I would like to thank Ms. Alaburic for having addressed this question with you. She addresses it through the events in Stupni Do. I have listened to her, and I have re-read the Military Disciplinary Code, P00425, which you don't have, I'm sure, in your documents. This could be placed on the screen, but I don't think it is necessary to look at it. I compared the former Yugoslavia text with the text of the ABiH and the text of the Croatian Army, and of the HVO, and I see that there isn't much difference between all these texts with the system of my country. There is very little difference. When an offence is committed -- afterwards, I would like you to answer, General Petkovic, please. When a military contravenes the system, this could be of two kinds. It could be of a disciplinary nature or it could be of a criminal nature. If it is of a disciplinary nature, it is defined under Article 3 of the Military Code. I'm not going to quote them all, but, for instance, this is the case of a soldier who refuses to obey an order. That comes under the military discipline rules of the army. That is the case, for instance, of a soldier who is not obeying the orders as he should. He's being asked to monitor the entrance door of the barracks, and in the middle of the night he is caught sleeping. That is a disciplinary offence. Eight are listed here in Article 3. And in Article 59, Article 59 provides that the commander of a unit can then punish the person in question. That is what we call a disciplinary breach. As far as crimes are concerned, General Petkovic, that is another story. When there is a crime, this does not come under Article 3 of the Military Disciplinary Code. When a crime is committed, and that is something which you will understand when I put questions to you later on, then the military prosecutor intervenes, or an investigating judge, and this has got nothing to do with the penalty imposed if it is a disciplinary breach. If you read the text as it stands, of course, it can happen that when a crime is committed, the commander places the soldier in custody and punishes him that way. He will then be placed in a military prison. But he can be taken into custody. According to the Military Disciplinary Code which you had in the JNA and in the HVO, did it coincide with the situation where a unit commander can punish a military who has committed a disciplinary breach to military discipline, but when a crime is committed, he can arrest him on a temporary basis, but then this falls within the competence of another jurisdiction? Am I right or am I wrong? You are totally free to answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, you're quite right, but I'd just like to add something. Infractions, offences, the first point you say, when somebody fails to carry out an order properly, in that case then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, I will let you take the floor. I could have completed my question by saying: As a prosecutor, I have sometimes had to manage cases in which military had committed crimes, and in cases like those the military in my country was not the subject of military disciplinary sanction because this fell under another jurisdiction. Because a commander was entitled to take him into custody, he then was the subject of another procedure, which was a criminal procedure, which was instigated by the prosecutor and not by the commander. Did things work like that in the JNA, in the HVO, and in the Croatian Army? You were fortunate enough, or unfortunate - I don't know - to have served in three armies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps even four, Your Honour. Yes, rules on military disciplinary action in force in the HVO was, well, the same as the one used in the Yugoslav People's Army and is the same as the rules and regulations that were in force in the Republic of Croatia. So there were two levels. The first level were lighter offences, where the commanders could mete out sanctions, but only to soldiers and soldiers in detention. Now, when it comes to proper detention, officers and non-commissioned officers could just be meted out light sentences, they could be given reprimands. But if an offence was considered more serious and jeopardised the life of a unit, both in the former JNA -- there were military disciplinary courts attached to military districts in Croatia, there were also military disciplinary courts. Herceg-Bosna enacted rules and regulations where military disciplinary courts are mentioned. However, they were not -- they were never established, because there were not the necessary cadres to set them up. Now, with the military disciplinary courts, there were several types of measures that could be meted out. First of all, you could be stopped or held back, or you could -- you would not be promoted for four years. You would have to wait four years for promotion. Now, if you had a two-year ban on promotion, then you would carry the rank you already held for six years. Furthermore, a decision could have been made to deduct 10 or 20 per cent from your salary for a maximum period of two years. That was another sanction. And then for officers and non-commissioned officers, there was detention up to 30 days that the Military Disciplinary Court could give. And for officers and NCOs, they could also be struck off the list of reserve officers. I think there was another measure that could have been implemented - I'm not quite sure - for officers. Well, they could also lose their rank. That was another measure. So those were basically the measures that could be applied both in the Yugoslav People's Army, when it came to military disciplinary courts, and these same measures were applied in the Republic of Croatia. And let me tell you that I was the president of the Military Disciplinary Court in Split, for example, for a time, for one term of office, and I know that there were sentences of that kind, too, measures of that kind. And this was also provided for by Herceg-Bosna in its rules and regulations. However, as I said, the military disciplinary courts were never actually established, attached to the operative zones or the Main Staff, and not every operative -- it needn't have been for every operative zone. You could have one military disciplinary court for several zones, and that was the case in Croatia while I was president of the Military Disciplinary Court. So Herceg-Bosna did not succeed in actually setting up courts of this kind, and in my opinion, because it failed to do so, the command structures were deprived of sanctions and measures that could be taken. Now, the third part of what you mentioned, when it came to crimes, crime and punishment, I think the proceedings were the same in the JNA and in the Croatian Army, and in Herceg-Bosna as well. If you know who the perpetrator or perpetrators were, then you were duty-bound to ensure that they did not abscond, which meant that you had to secure him, and block off the crime scene, if I can put it that way, where the crime took place. You would have to collect up all the evidence and gather all the information, and then report that to the investigating judge. If the perpetrators were unknown and a crime had been committed, then you had the Security Service at your disposal, as well as the military police, who would then undertake the process of investigating the matter, and once again it would end up with the investigating judge, or, rather, further proceedings would be taken within the various structures. So the rules and regulations and provisions were the same both in the JNA -- I think Croatia copied out that section of the law, and it applied in Herceg-Bosna as well, except that major drawback, and that is to say that no military disciplinary courts were actually established. And then there was this third method, which was one applied in the JNA and in the Republic of Croatia, and it was also prescribed for Herceg-Bosna, and a basis was formed with the military district courts and that system that were in several locations to deal with it that way. So since we're mentioning three states, three countries, those provisions were, to all intents and purposes, well, I would say even identical, and the procedures and measures that could be taken were also identical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you, General Petkovic, for this very exhaustive reply. And given that you touched on disciplinary sanctions, I realise that you chaired a disciplinary commission and/or a military disciplinary court, and therefore you know more than anybody else what it's all about. So thank you very much for giving us this information. Just a small point of clarification. When I said that you were part of three armies, I was basing that on the facts that I was sure of, but, in fact, you may have been a member of a fourth army, which would be the ABiH. But, of course, this will be in the judgement. And you will understand that I could not take any position on this point, and this is why I only talked about three armies. I'm being very cautious when I put anything forward. But we take note of the fact that you were a member of four armies. Ms. Alaburic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Document 4D75, General, your letter to Sefer Halilovic. It's in the third set of documents, the last-but-one; the third binder, that is. But maybe you can rely on e-court. I will read out the section in which I'm interested in now and ask you for your comment. In February 1993, among other things, you wrote to Sefer Halilovic, I quote: "I looked forward to each new soldier, Croatian or Muslim, because I knew that they had a common goal. The HVO hasn't changed its attitude or behaviour towards the BH Army to this day. We are aware that with the present balance of powers, neither the HVO nor the BH Army alone can defeat the Chetniks." Could you please comment, General, on what I have just read?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honours. I can say that I was pleased when I saw that the BH Army was growing stronger and that it would be able to stand up to the Serb forces. I was also pleased by the HVO growing stronger, and also proud of the fact that the HVO had some Muslims in its ranks. In spite of some tensions, I sincerely wished that Sefer Halilovic succeed to get to terms with the Chetniks or -- in Central Bosnia. I enjoyed -- or, rather, I promised him that we would engage additional forces of ours and also move up to the front against the Chetniks.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did you ever invite any prominent persons from the BH Army to come to the HVO staff?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When Hujka received the brigade, once it was established, I wanted Halilovic [as interpreted] to come and see, and we wanted to keep Jasmin Jaganjac in the HVO and give him an opportunity to rise or be promoted maybe even up to the higher levels. And I can mention one more person, Mirsad Catic from Konjic. I asked Arif to lend him to me, and he was for -- my deputy in the JNA for a while. But he had also an injured leg, so we wanted to give him the opportunity to be treated in Split if he came to the HVO to help us out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I would like to ask General Petkovic about one issue to be clarified. In the transcript, it is said that: "I asked Arif to lend him," that is Mirsad Catic, "to lend him to me, and my deputy in the JNA ..." I believe that you said that he was your deputy in the JNA, but it is again not very clear if it was Catic or Arif, that is, Arif Pasalic, who was your deputy before in the JNA. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. First I said that in Mostar we wanted Arif to join us in the HVO Main Staff, because we had a brigade and appointed a new commander. We made that request to the political structures in Mostar with who we were in permanent contact. But when they told us that they were establishing a corps and that Arif has his place there, I met Mr. Catic in Konjic, and I asked them to let him at least come to my Main Staff, because this Mr. Catic was my deputy in the JNA for a while and I wanted to have him next to me. And, secondly, I believe that he stepped on a land-mine, or something happened to him, anyway, so I could have given him the opportunity to get treatment in Split for this leg of his.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your answer. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to correct the transcript on the previous page, 29, line 22. General Petkovic said that they called Arif Pasalic, rather than Halilovic, as is recorded in this transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now tell the Trial Chamber, sir, what was your attitude toward the alleged idea that part of Bosnia-Herzegovina separate itself from that country and become part of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My attitude? I never was in favour of part of Bosnia-Herzegovina seceding from that state and becoming part of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General, we saw a document dated 21 April 1993. It's P2019. Judge Antonetti prepared it for your examination; I didn't. It was -- these were the minutes of Tihomir Blaskic taken at your meeting in Zenica, and there Sefer Halilovic told you something: "Hey, what are you talking about? You only want a Croatian state in these parts, anyway." And then you spoke your mind about the so-called Greater Croatia. So could you now please explain to the Trial Chamber what you thought about this idea and the possibility of its being implemented ?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me first say what I replied to Halilovic. I said to him, You must be out of your mind if you really think that's the case. Croatia has as an integral part of its territory the Serbian Krajina which wishes to leave Croatia, and it is a crazy idea to think that Croatia, given this unsolved problem, aspires to anything more; something along those lines. So I'm not sure whether it was -- how faithfully it was recorded in that document. But, anyway, as far as I'm concerned, I was never in favour of the idea that part of Bosnia-Herzegovina should join Croatia. Instead, Bosnia-Herzegovina was a unified country and stayed this way, only I'm sorry that nowadays they can't seem to be able to run their own affairs.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What is your attitude toward the relationship between the HVO and the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before you answer this question, I would like to come back to Halilovic. Listen carefully, General Praljak -- I'm sorry, General Petkovic. But I was thinking of General Praljak, and you'll understand why. When General Praljak was in your stead, when you were not there, General Praljak talked about General Halilovic. I do not have the transcript before me because I was not planning to put this question to you right now. And I don't always look at the transcript, anyway, but I trust my memory. In a couple of words, and General Praljak had said the following. He had explained that Halilovic and others were sometimes pushing Alija Izetbegovic to voice some views or take some positions, and I think I understood - I may be wrong, but this is what I understood through what General Praljak said - that he may have some words against General Halilovic, but at the same time he thought highly of you. But against Halilovic, he had none. So he said the following: According to him, General Halilovic, who was, like you, a member of the JNA before, was playing such a game that one could believe that he was playing in the hands of the Serbian KOS, and one could think that he was a Serbian agent that had been infiltrated in the ABiH. So these were very strong words that were uttered by General Praljak. So now you have been on the ground, you have seen General Halilovic, you have spoken to him probably in Geneva, and I assume that you must have had lunch or dinners with him, so what do you think of the opinion expressed by General Praljak on General Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I can very briefly say -- speak my mind without either confirming or rejecting General Praljak's view. To my mind, General Halilovic did not work either for the JNA or for Yugoslavia. He broke all bands with the JNA and Yugoslavia. I know that from heated meetings called by General Morillon and many others. And that -- and the same situation prevailed in Geneva when we spoke to Mr. Nambiar. General Halilovic, if you ask me, never shed a tear for Yugoslavia or the JNA. And as for Mladic, he didn't have a nice word for him, and there is footage to that effect. Halilovic is a few years younger than I. He was a security officer for a while, and he served in Djakovo, which is in Slavonia, in the east of Croatia. But I don't think that whoever worked for the Security Service automatically was a KOS man, because the Security Service was separate from the Counter-Intelligence Service, KOS. The Security Service worked inside a unit and worked locally, whereas the KOS worked even across borders. I heard the stories from some people of him being a KOS man, but I wouldn't say that of him. He had his views, he opted for Bosnia-Herzegovina, and he was very critical of Mladic and his team that accompanied him to meetings and talks. As for him and Mr. Izetbegovic, I heard from Mr. Morillon when he said to me, on the 9th of June, You won't be speaking to Halilovic today because great things are going on in Sarajevo; the 1st Corps is on its feet because Halilovic is to be replaced, but he couldn't be replaced in five minutes because they had to persuade all the other commanders, and that went on all day. But why Mr. Izetbegovic decide to replace Halilovic has remained a mystery to me to this date. Halilovic -- or, rather, Mr. Izetbegovic [as interpreted] always wanted to impose himself. He was very assertive. He always wanted to be number 1, even at Presidency's meetings, and not everybody was willing to accept that, so that obviously a rift came about between the two of them. I cannot say that Halilovic was a KOS agent. His mind worked very differently. By the way, there were stories of me being a KOS man because I had come from the JNA, although that has nothing to do with reality. I know that he worked for the Security Service. It was the security service of a brigade, but I know what their tasks are. It is limited to some operational tasks and tactical tasks, whereas the KOS even works in other countries. So I never accepted these arguments or stories, but he was very assertive, he was indeed. You agreed to him about one thing, and when the following -- when the course of the discussion didn't seem to go in his favour, then he would change his mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Yes, your position has been recorded in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a correction on page 34, line 6. The general said that Sefer Halilovic wanted to impose himself at Presidency meetings, rather than Mr. Izetbegovic, as is recorded here, and that other people objected to that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed, that was the case. Actually, I heard those stories from other people in the ABiH when I asked why he had left.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I believe that we have two more minutes to go. What do you think of the relationship between the HVO and the Armed Forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The Armed Forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina, General.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you ask me, the HVO was an integral part of the Armed Forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and we were waiting for the man we considered the commander-in-chief of the Armed Forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina to gather everybody around him and say publicly, on TV, Today it is we who represent the Armed Forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Petkovic isn't here, but in his stead there is so-and-so, et cetera. Mr. Izetbegovic spent a day and a half in Mostar, and he was in a position to do that in October 1992, or -- and he could have done that whenever he wanted, in Geneva and when I was in Jablanica with him. But he was the president of the country and the commander-in-chief, and, you know, this should have been his initiative.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us about the joint command of the HVO and the ABiH. We saw a number of documents here, and we know that this joint command couldn't be established before the signing of the Washington Agreements. Did the HVO in any way obstruct the establishing of a joint command of the HVO and the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We considered the joint command a great step forward, and we also saw it as something that provided us security, because we were in a weaker position than the ABiH. So that was a guarantee of our survival. But some things happened at the political level. The Vance-Owen Plan failed for good, and then things went bad.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: By way of finishing, General, tell us, the two years you spent in Bosnia-Herzegovina, what did you think -- which country were you defending there?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I defended Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I left that country. It is still in existence today, so -- it exists in its original borders, so nobody took any part of its territory from it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, General. Your Honours, thank you for additional time. I believe my time is up, so thank you once more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed, you have used six hours and forty minutes. This was confirmed by the Registrar. So Mr. Scott will have six hours and forty minutes, as it was planned. We will have a break, because it's nearly 20 to 4.00. We will resume at 4.00, and we will go until 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I have understood correctly, you have completed your examination-in-chief, Ms. Alaburic. I wanted to specify, for information purposes for the Praljak Defence, a document was unaccounted for because the document couldn't be printed out, I believe. For some time now, when documents are being copied, some of the numbers don't always come out properly. This would be 3D03640, 640. I believe that's the right number. Mr. Kovacic, you can look at this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, Your Honour, we will take a look in the course of the day, I hope.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as the oral decision we took yesterday pertaining to the extension of time so that the English translation is provided and that people can make their submissions after that, that applies to all and everyone, not only for the Praljak Defence. This stands to reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, I shall now put you a number of questions. We have been sitting in this courtroom for the last four years now. On several occasions, and too rarely, in my view, we have been able to talk to each other. I now have some time before me, and I'm going to put you a series of questions. Let's begin today. As you know, there will be two hours left when we finish. I shall resume on Monday. I don't think I'll be able to finish on, so we might still be addressing this on Tuesday, part of the hearing on Tuesday. To all Defence counsel and to the Prosecutor, I have handed out the documents relating to the questions I was going to ask. And to be fair, I relied on the Prosecution's case, based on the Prosecution documents that bear the letter P, as well as the Defence case and its various submissions. I relied on documents which are either D3, D4, D2, and sometimes I relied on P documents as well, because these are documents that can be used by either. When I shall address the documents and when I shall dedicate my time to the Prosecution's case, to begin with, I may also highlight in a document some elements which could be deemed exculpatory, and vice versa. This is an empirical division I'm making. A document can be read in different ways. Before we start, there are a few preliminary questions I'd like to address. As you know, you come after General Praljak, who has already taken the stand before you. I have not spent the same time on him, because General Praljak testified at great length and I realised afterwards that I had spent approximately 22 hours with him. Out of these 22 hours, a lot of time had been spent on the presidential transcripts, so it is not useful to address these presidential transcripts again, with one exception which I will address at the end of the first day, namely, on Monday, which seems to be a very important transcript, in my view. Let me give everyone the number. That is P07475. This is the presidential transcripts of the 4th of June, 1994, and there are three people present; Tudjman, Susak, Bobetko. And you are also mentioned. That is why this transcript is important. So we will have an opportunity to address this again. General Petkovic, as you know, I put questions to General Praljak, and a Judge in this Tribunal, when he puts questions, he or she must be extremely careful when the questions are put, because at no point in time must it transpire that the Judge has an opinion on the guilt or non-guilt of an accused. That is certainly the reason why very few Judges put questions since the inception of this Tribunal 15 years ago. There can be a number of reasons for that. Perhaps they are not sufficiently experienced in criminal trials, shy away from putting questions; I don't know. But when there is a question put by a Judge, the Judge is running a very great risk by so doing. I must say that when I put a question once, I got a very spontaneous reaction on the part of Mr. Karnavas. I did not understand his reaction. There was a witness who was sitting where you are sitting now, and the question I asked was: How had he been convened to meetings which were of a presidential nature; was there an agenda or something? And I wanted to know how this functioned. And Mr. Karnavas stood up right away, and I didn't understand why he had stood up and spoken so forcefully. That is the first time in 30 years that a lawyer stood up in that manner, whereas I was just putting a question -- an innocent question and asking how the meeting was unfolding, was there an agenda, and this is what happened. I believe that another person would have said, All right, I won't put anymore questions, but I decided to continue putting my questions in a courageous manner. You must noticed, General Petkovic, that my questions are very lengthy questions. When I put questions, I want to make sure that the person who is going to answer the question has all the information. I don't want to direct the witness in one way or another, so I give the witness all the information I actually have. Sometimes I open up several avenues for the witness, and I don't exclude anything. Therefore, General Petkovic, when you answer, you have the opportunity to answer in any way you like. If, in the question I put, you notice a mistake, do not hesitate to let me know in that case, because I'm not infallible and I can make mistakes; all the more so that we are discussing extremely technical topics, military topics, where it is important sometimes to have a lot of knowledge on military matters and detailed knowledge. Since you are a high-ranking officer and a general, you have held high commanding positions, and this may be a handicap for a regular judge. If I make a mistake when I put my question, please do not hesitate to let me know, and I shall welcome any correction. I don't wish to have an answer to a question which hasn't been put properly. Could your answers also be as comprehensive as possible. This is an important moment for you. You have waited for this for a number of years. Everyone can put themselves in your shoes, and for you this is a very important moment in your life. And I understand full well that you wish to answer the questions. General Petkovic, this is my question: What is your status? You are an accused, but you are testifying as a witness, and you have taken the solemn declaration. Admittedly, when I discovered in the Rules that the accused had to take the solemn declaration, this raised a number of questions in my mind, because in my system - and I believe in your system it was the same - an accused does not take the solemn declaration, but here in this Tribunal an accused must take the solemn declaration. So the accused should be telling the truth, but sometimes there might be a number of issues. I'll give you an example. For instance, if I put a question to you and you say to me, I don't wish to answer the question because this could incriminate me, in that case, if I apply the theory of the witness-witness, and I will say, Yes, please answer, because you will not be prosecuted. And then you will turn around and say, Well, all right, in that village or that village, I admit that, which that means that you cannot be prosecuted, you're exonerated. This is something strange, which probably escaped the Judges who drafted this provision. I'm speaking off my own bat. You are an accused who is testifying, and since you have taken the solemn declaration, you should be telling the truth. So as you know, General Petkovic, Mr. Praljak -- the Praljak Defence has asked to have some time to cross-examine you, as submissions have been filed. When I heard that this time application had been made, I thought that General Praljak wanted to put questions to you as part of the time that had been allocated to him. In legal terms, I looked into the matter. As far as I know, unless I'm mistaken, this case has never arisen in any of the international trials. No accused has ever addressed questions to another accused. In Nuremberg, this didn't happen; in Tokyo, not either. In Cambodia, with the ongoing trials, not either. In Lebanon, not at all, because the trials haven't started yet. At ICC, it's still in the making, so we don't have examples yet of this. And if I turn to the common law countries, the trials are usually single trials. The question doesn't arise. And in civil law, trials in my country, for instance, an accused cannot examine another accused. I've never had such a case, so this is the first time, and this will be the first time. In my view, the answer can only be found in the Statute. The Statute states that an accused can examine or have an accused examined. "Examined" means himself. If he has someone examined, that means the examination is conducted by counsel. As the Statute provides for this, I, therefore, hold that General Praljak may put questions to you, but this will only be pursuant to Article 21 of the Statute. I have found nothing as far as case law is concerned. The Rules of Procedure and Evidence says nothing about this, and we have no examples to date. We only have this article in the Statute. After having hesitated quite a lot, I feel that if General Praljak so wishes - I don't know if he does - that he may put questions to you. In addition, I would like to recall that you're presumed innocent. This is important. It's important to state this, and it's important to reassert this, because contrary to the feeling you may have had, General Petkovic, we, the Judges, we have not deliberated on either the facts nor on the responsibility. We have not met to discuss these issues, and we will only meet once the trial is over, once we have the submissions of the Prosecutor and Defence counsel. We cannot say that we know which way the trial is going. We cannot, because I have not discussed with the other Judges the question of your responsibility or innocence, and we haven't discussed the facts either. This is something we will do when the time comes to deliberate, which means that when I put a question to you, this is solely my question I am putting to you. I have not proffered the questions and met with my colleagues beforehand. I haven't even given them my list of questions. And I haven't given them my list of documents, either, to make sure that I am really independent. If there's something which you may doubt, I'd like to remind you that I was a confirmation Judge. This is something I told General Praljak at the time. I confirmed the indictment. You were not there at the time. One fine morning, somebody knocked on my door to bring me all the documents relating to this case. There were cubic metres of documents. And 24 hours before that, President Meron told me that I had been appointed Judge in this case. I thought I would be the Presiding Judge in the Popovic case, because I had been the Pre-Trial Judge in the Popovic case and I was about to become the Presiding Judge in the Popovic case, and one fine morning somebody knocks on my door to bring me these cubic metres of documents. Today, this is something which we should know. I have nothing to hide. I am fully transparent. This is something you should know. When people bring you cubic metres of documents and when you are asked to confirm all of this, things have to be done swiftly. So what did I do then? I checked that there was a legal foundation for this, as regards the counts that were mentioned, and I made sure that there was one document -- that there were documents which coincided with this, documents that confirmed what was in the indictment, but that there was a nexus, a connection on a prima facie basis, and that is how I confirmed the indictment. I must tell you that if I were to be seized today of such matter, i.e., to confirm an indictment, I would proceed differently. This would no longer be the case, because since 2008 no more indictments can be issued. And what is missing is this: The list of all the exhibits should have been annexed to the indictment, and that was not the case. So we do not have an entire list of exhibits, and today I can't tell you, from memory, what exhibits were presented in support of the indictment because these exhibits were in the thousands and there was no list of the exhibits. So if we were to improve the system, that would be something that should be done. The ICC is going in that direction, and the ICC, when they hand down the confirmation of the indictment, they also provide a reasoned opinion. I confirmed the indictment and I signed the arrest warrant, because when there is an indictment, there is an arrest warrant, and I signed the arrest warrant for you. After that, when I learnt that I was to be a Pre-Trial Judge during a status conference, General Praljak was present, he had problems with his lawyers; at the time, he was alone. I then raised the issue of a potential withdrawal. Since I had been the Judge involved in the confirmation of the indictment, could I be conducting the trial? I quoted this Tribunal's case law. No one objected, and I continued with this. Had someone objected, I would have left the case right away. There was no point in having any problems when I had not been asked to conduct this case. In addition, I also checked whether the indictment and General Gotovina, there wasn't some kind of connection. This is something I'm sure you're familiar with. In my country, I needed to try Mr. Gotovina for an ordinary offence, and my name appeared in the Gotovina proceedings. This is something I discovered afterwards, and I discovered afterwards that I had tried General Gotovina. I then asked to withdraw from the Cermak-Markac case, because Mr. Gotovina was involved in that case. To begin with, as Mr. Gotovina was a fugitive, then that was not necessary. Once he was arrested, the President then changed the Judges, and I was no longer appointed to that case, because I feel that if a Judge has any form of connection with a case, the Judge in question should withdraw automatically without a request or application being filed to that effect. I knew nothing about those events. I had not been in contact whatsoever with the accused. And, moreover, I'd never been to Bosnia-Herzegovina, so I was neutral in this case. You may have a few doubts about those people who are going to try you. You will be tried by me, through the evidence adduced by the Prosecutor, who, beyond all reasonable doubt, must convince us that you are guilty, and the documents of the Prosecution, of the Defence, of witness testimony, need to be scrutinised. And at the end of this, normally speaking, the truth should rise to the surface. This is something I wanted to share with you before you answer my questions. I've stated this before. My questions are not trick questions. That's not how I'll proceed. In my job, I have always held everyone in great respect, whether it be an accused or any other person. It's not because a person is accused that he should be well less-treated than any other person. You are a human being. You are entitled to respect, in light of the high positions you held before coming here. No later than a few moments ago, I discovered that you presided over a disciplinary court. All the more reason to show you respect. Also, you are testifying under oath. So, General Petkovic, let me start off with a question which was put a few moments ago, something which didn't come to mind, but this was Ms. Alaburic's last question, so I shall therefore use her last question and start with mine. You said, when answering Ms. Alaburic's question, that you defended the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, so I would like you to explain to me -- unlike General Praljak, who was born in Bosnia-Herzegovina, you were born in Croatia, so what I would like to know is why, as a Croat, you volunteered at some stage, when you joined the HVO, to defend this Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina within the framework of the HVO. What was your deepest motivation? Was that for personal reasons, was that a very strong motivation coming from yourself, or was there any other reason? Could you perhaps explain that to me?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, it was exclusively for personal reasons. I agreed to go to Bosnia-Herzegovina and to defend the Republic of Croatia on that territory, to defend Bosnia-Herzegovina or, rather, to stand up to the aggression of the Bosnian Serbs and the then Yugoslav People's Army. I considered that in this way, I could make a greater contribution to the defence of the southern part of the Republic of Croatia and the defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, because a safe and secure Bosnia-Herzegovina on that territory meant that a large portion of the Republic of Croatia would be secure and safe, too, because it borders on Bosnia-Herzegovina. At the time, I occupied operative functions, operative posts, and I considered that at the given time and in view of the experience that I had gained in the war on the territory of the former Yugoslavia, in this case the Republic of Croatia, that I could give far more to the Republic of Croatia, and thereby to Bosnia-Herzegovina, if I were to cross over the border and become involved in the defence system on that territory. So that was my guiding light. And it's true I don't have anything much to do with Bosnia-Herzegovina; a few relatives and friends here and there, perhaps, but during my lifetime I just spent a few months in Bosnia-Herzegovina in three or four locations, but seeing what was happening there in Bosnia-Herzegovina and seeing the movements towards the Republic of Croatia, and envisaging what could happen if Bosnia and Herzegovina were to be closed off at that sole entrance point, I simply decided to leave everything I'd been doing in the Croatian Army behind and, for a time, to relocate and go to Bosnia-Herzegovina. And I think that by doing that, I contributed to a great extent to the defence of the Republic of Croatia, itself, because the forces that were going to move against the Republic of Croatia were stopped in Bosnia-Herzegovina. In that way, we expressed our solidarity with Bosnia and Herzegovina and its nations and ethnicities and provided one sole entrance -- the one sole entrance into Bosnia-Herzegovina remained open. We provided access. So that's what prompted me to go to Bosnia-Herzegovina, nothing else but thoughts along those lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. If I understand correctly, because when you make a long statement, and I actually encourage you to do so because the clock is not ticking as far as you're concerned, so you can make long answers, but I have to summarise in order to understand perfectly what you're saying and in order to avoid making any mistakes. The fact that you volunteered to go to Bosnia-Herzegovina was due to the fact that for you it was a way of securing Croatia, because if that part was going to fall, it would endanger the whole of Croatia, and so you felt it was your duty to be a volunteer. Did I understand your statement correctly?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's precisely it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'm going to touch on a sensitive issue, and you know that I never shy away from touching on sensitive issues. If you want to, we can move to private session. Otherwise, we can stay in open session. For the time being, we are in open session. You testified twice; in June 1999, in the Blaskic case, and in November 2000, in the Kordic case. During your two testimonies, you were a witness of the Court, but I understood that you were a witness of the Court because the Croat government was actually very reluctant at the time for any officers to testify, and the Croatian government was very reluctant and not very akin to co-operate, and therefore the technical solution was to bring you to the stand as a witness of the Court, with another specificity, because there was a videolink. Is that correct or is that incorrect?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, that is not correct. If anybody in the Blaskic case, be it the Defence or the Prosecution, had called me to testify, I would have answered the call. I expected the Blaskic Defence to want me to come and testify, but they never asked me to do so; nor did the OTP. And at that moment, I got a summons from the Trial Chamber. Probably both parties were in accordance with that, and the Trial Chamber considered it necessary for me to come. So the entire procedure is not true. I was prepared to come and testify for either party, but what I expected least finally came true. I was summoned by the Trial Chamber. Only at a late stage in the proceedings did it occur to me that something like that might happen. I don't know whether the Republic of Croatia prevented anybody from going to The Hague to testify. Probably they wouldn't have been able to do so, only possibly if the Defence had wanted anybody to come and testify; then they could have prevented that. So this is all I can tell you about my first evidence. And as far as my second evidence is concerned --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
