utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will stay on this. Is it true that you asked to have protection measures? And if so, why did you ask that?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I was least involved in that process because I simply didn't know. I simply heard that Croatia --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak -- sorry, General Petkovic. I keep saying "General Praljak" because he was before me for days and days, and it's difficult for me to get used to you, but I'm sure I will, eventually. I have the transcript before me. This is the transcript of the beginning of your testimony, and here is what it says. It's the Presiding Judge, Judge Jorda, who is speaking, and he greets you, and then he says the following. It's page 22440: "General Petkovic wanted to testify through a videolink, under technical conditions, which seems to be quite usual." So my question is the following: Why did you want to testify through a videolink?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, this suggestion was made to me by the representatives of the Croatian government in charge of the co-operation with the ICTY, because they said that they had agreed with the Tribunal for this to be arranged in that manner. And then I accepted that. Croatia at that time had a rather lengthy correspondence with the Tribunal, and when I heard about these technical measures, I said, Okay, it's all the same to me. If you want, I can testify from Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Still on this same page in the transcript, the Presiding Judge says the following: "It means that General Petkovic wanted to benefit from protective measures." This is what I read, so I don't understand. You are saying, No, while the Presiding Judge says that you required or you requested protective measures. So could you please clarify this?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I didn't know what kind of reply to give, and at that time it was suggested to me by the Croatian government that I should request protective measures, that nothing will happen to me. And they also suggested that I should apply for a private session. That was all. And they said something else to me, You will not testify there alone; you'll be accompanied by an attorney of the Republic of Croatia and a representative of the Croatian government. I think that was the first instance in which a witness was to be controlled by the government, but it was put that way to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. This is very true, what you're saying. Your hearing was different to what is happening today. The Chamber had given you a number of points and gave you some time to make a presentation, and after that, instead of asking questions like I'm doing, they asked the Prosecutor to put some questions to you, and then to the Defence team, and Judges also asked a few questions. And you may remember this little detail. Judge Shahabuddeen asked you if the soldiers and yourself who were in Bosnia-Herzegovina were paid by the Republic of Croatia, and then the representative of the Croatian government stood up and said, He cannot answer this question. Do you remember this anecdote?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I remember. I remember that my minister of defence explained to me for an hour how this would go on, They have the right to interrupt you and tell you that you shouldn't reply. And, yes, at a certain moment the man stood up and said, I believe -- No, we don't want the general to answer those questions. He really intervened that way. And it took the minister an hour to explain that to me, that I would find myself in such a situation. And I asked him then, Well, Minister, what does the government think, that I'm testifying in the Blaskic case or in a case of the Republic of Croatia? I now really don't know who's being tried up there. And he said, No, it is my duty to point this out to you. We were able to achieve that your evidence is monitored by a representative of government and a lawyer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. In November 2000, a year later, you testify in the Kordic case. Could you please tell us under which circumstances you were called to the Bar during the Kordic case?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the attorney - what was his name - Naumovski, at a moment -- at this one moment in time made an appointment with me to speak to me in Split, and we spoke for an hour and a half. And he said, We agreed you to be a witness in the Kordic case. And I believe that I was to testify in April of that year. And I said to him, Sir, my daughter is getting married in April, and going to the Tribunal and then returning, and I've already given evidence there once, no, I can't do that. And that's how we parted. I didn't receive any news from him for a while, but then I received a phone call from him in which he asked me what I thought of that. And I said to him, No, I cannot go there and testify the way you expect me to, because I need some time for preparation. And then they gave up on me. I never confirmed that I would be his witness. I think I told him that I could be a Chamber witness, which may have been the most useful solution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you were called to testify in the Kordic case. I'm not going to give the name of the witness, because it was a protected witness, but you noted that there were documents that were put forward by the Office of the Prosecutor. Could you tell us, under oath, whether during both cases, Blaskic and Kordic cases, and in this very trial, could you tell us if a group called The Hague Group coming from the Croatian government could have done anything or would have put pressure on you in order to, quote/unquote, "prepare" your coming to The Hague, or whether nothing happened; you were helped when you asked for help, but you enjoyed the entirety of your freedom when you testified? Could you tell us about this, if you know about this? Of course, if you don't know anything, then you can tell us, and then we can move to something else.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can say this to you: I said so in the Kordic case already. I had nothing to do with The Hague Group or Mr. Rebic. I said that the gentleman who represented the government when I gave evidence, Mr. Udiljak, called me three or four times about the articles published in the Croatian press. Do you read those articles, General? What do you say to that? And I replied, It seems to me that somebody staged a trial or a presentation of that trial to the Croatian public, but they diverged somewhat from what's going on in the courtroom, although I didn't really know what was going on in the courtroom. There was some malignant articles about special-purpose units or military police units, which were called various names, but in no articles that I read was there any mention of that. That was my only contact with the team of the Croatian government for the co-operation with the ICTY, but never with Mr. Rebic, and nobody of them ever mentioned Petkovic. After I received the first call, I went to Split, said, Goodbye, to the minister. I never even went to lunch with him, because he only spoke to me about somebody representing Croatian, in the interests, without bothering to ask me how I felt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'm now going to talk about your family background, because in my country, when someone is accused, we are looking at the person's character, we have psychological experts, we have medical experts, psychiatric experts, and we have all sorts of information that we use. Here, we have nothing. We have a name, and if the person doesn't say anything, in fact, we don't really know who we're dealing with. And, in fact, I would like to get to know you a little bit. I would like to know who you are. So could you perhaps tell me what were your parents doing, what profession did they have? Could you tell me a little bit about your family background?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. My father was a railroad worker, a common worker. My mother, for the first two years, until the age of 22, worked, but then gave up her job to be a housewife. I have two brothers. One is five years younger than I, and the other is ten years younger than I. They still live in Vrpolje, which is 10 kilometres away from Sibenik. They live with my mother. My father died three years ago. So I'm from a working-class family, and this may have been one of the reasons why I decided to enroll on a military school, because my father didn't have the means to pay for my education. Apart from that, he also supported my grandmother and grandfather, who didn't have an income, so he was the only source of income in our family. So I graduated from secondary school, and then I joined the army, the JNA, but my first choice was the navy. The contract with the JNA was that I had to spend twice the length of my education as a career officer, and that was, indeed, my plan. Although I'm from Dalmatia and it would have been logical for the JNA to accept me in the navy, they wanted me to serve in the army. I had two uncles who were in the JNA, and my father had also served in that army. And I finally accepted their proposal, although I was -- I did consider refusing because they didn't grant my wish. I went to Belgrade to Military Academy in 1961. One of my brothers is an engineer who works at the aluminium factory in Sibenik, or the former aluminium factory. I don't know who's the owner now, after the privatization. But, anyway, he still has a job, although he's afraid he might lose it, like many others in Croatia. He has two children. One is a university student, and the other is in primary school. The younger brother works for the railroad as technical staff. He's also married. He has two children. One of his sons got married recently, so they are all grown up. This is my family from my father's and my mother's side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How many children do you have, and what is their profession?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have two children, two daughters. Both are married. One works for a bank, and so does the other. My older son-in-law is a dentist, a private practitioner, and my younger son-in-law is also a bank employee. I have two grandchildren. One is in the first class of primary school, and the younger one still has four years to go. He's only three. My wife retired a number of years ago. She wasn't old enough to retire, but she decided to retire prematurely for health reasons. And now she is looking after her grandchildren. I have an apartment of my own, and both my daughters have their own apartments and cars, and both families make an independent living.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, if I remember well, you attended the wedding of one of your daughters - I'm sure this was your youngest daughter - when you were granted provisional release. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it was granted to me then, and I thank you for that. I swapped with a colleague of mine to be able to go when my daughter was getting married. Actually, they were waiting whether I would get leave before she set the date of her marriage. That's my younger daughter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Last time, I put the question to you, and you provided a very lengthy answer, but I wish to get back to this. When you left the JNA to join the Croatian Army, I assume that this was an important moment in your life. But I had asked you whether you were a member of the Communist Party in Yugoslavia at the time, and you answered by saying, Yes, because in order to have a career, it was necessary to be a member of the Communist Party, of the Yugoslav Communist Party. In the Yugoslav system, those people who reached the top, either in the army, or in the judiciary, or in diplomacy, or in the administration, did these people necessarily have to be members of the Communist Party?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe that in all walks of life, that meant a lot. It wasn't absolutely required, but it meant a lot. In the Yugoslav People's Army, there was agitation for all officers and NCOs to become party members, and efforts were made for everybody to join the party. And I must say that the strongest party organisation, with the largest number of party numbers, was the JNA. I think it was stronger than any party organisation in any of the republics of the former Yugoslavia, at least as far as I know. And let me tell you one more thing. The head of the Committee of the Federal Secretariat of People's Defence, or National Defence, was a general, so under the level of division, that was no longer the case, because somebody would have the regular duties and next to that they would also go about their party duties. But at this highest level, you would only have your party duties exclusively.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, when I questioned General Praljak, I put to him a number of questions based on the Constitution of Yugoslavia, of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and of Croatia. This was some constitutional work I did. On looking at the Yugoslav Constitution, since you were an officer in the JNA, I was struck by the fact that the Yugoslav Army took into account ethnic specificities, i.e., Serb, Croat, Muslim. So this was taken into account. When you were in command in the JNA, was this true to fact or was this just something you mentioned in the documents and everybody asked themselves the question?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, that was really the situation. There were some quotas. Based on this or that number, it would be desirable to have a certain number of Serbs in the rank of colonel, and so-and-so many Croats or Muslims, et cetera, so the share of officer ethnicity was desirable, but it wasn't always fully possible to implement that. Croats weren't as eager to join the army than the Serbs. Slovenians were even less eager to do so, and there were -- the fewest were Kosovo Albanians. So there was much effort invested to have some Kosovo Albanians join in order to keep up that ethnic balance, but it was never up to the desired level. As for Croats, their share was about 12 per cent, and that is a very small number compared to the overall share of Croats in the then Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Under the aegis of Marshal Tito, who was a Croat, within the JNA, if you were a Croat, did that mean that you were promoted faster, or did this have no impact because of the quota system and everybody had their turn?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, the fact that Tito was a Croat didn't mean much. I think the most generals from Croatia were from a region called Lika, but they weren't Croats but ethnic Serbs. So if -- and when your seven or eight generals were to be promoted, there were efforts to have a certain balance, to have, let's say, two Croats and one Slovenian, but then there would be also three Serbs, because they were the most numerous ethnicity in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you exercised command within the JNA, as part of your training, all the training you underwent in the JNA, did you attend any training courses abroad in the Eastern Bloc, as it was called - in Hungary, for instance - Eastern Bloc countries? Did you go abroad to see how the other armies operated, how command was organised, and what the practices were, or was your training solely done within the Yugoslav Army?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, there was a so-called exchange of persons at certain levels in training. I never went abroad, but there were some people who went to the Soviet Union - there weren't many, though - and possibly to other Eastern Bloc countries where there were military schools. But I know that some went to the Soviet Union. One of my bosses, while I was a teacher, also graduated from the Artillery and Ballistics School, I believe it was called, in Russia, and he was my superior, so some officers did go; not very many, but some exchange existed. Likewise, the JNA trained some personnel from other countries. But as far as I remember, nobody came from the West then. Some were from non-aligned countries, and others were members of movements, such as the Polisario, or Arafat's men, Libyans, especially in the navy, and for three months, I had the chance to teach artillery to a group of Libyans.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: With your permission, Mr. President, I would only like to say that according to my knowledge, and of course I do not claim to be an expert on these issues, mainly in the 1960s, 1970s, and later on, too, a number of Yugoslav officers went also to the West, mainly to the United States and to other countries. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to thank my colleague for having specified this. This was to be my next question. I wanted to know whether officers of the Yugoslav Army went to the West, i.e., France or the United States. I wanted to know whether there was any co-operation with the West.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, Judge Prandler's right. It was a time -- although, actually, at that time I wasn't in the JNA, and if I was, I was a cadet, a low-ranking army man. It was at the time when tensions were high with Russia and when the West helped in arms and materiel, helped Yugoslavia. You have Shermans, the Howitzers, 155 Howitzers, and other weapons that arrived from the West as a sort of reward to the Yugoslav leadership, who distanced itself from the Russians, and to deflate, perhaps, a threat from the East towards Yugoslavia. And at the time, some people did go, but not in large numbers. They did go to the West, but not in large numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Last question on this topic. You, yourself, when you were serving in the JNA, did you take part in any military operations, operation manoeuvres, with other countries? Did you take part in any of these large manoeuvres? These were peaceful, of course, but these were military manoeuvres.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, I did not participate in that. I was a candidate on one occasion for a peace operation, I think it was, after the latest Israel-Lebanese war, but a colleague went instead of me. And in some exercises -- no, I didn't take part in any such exercises. And to be quite frank, I can't remember whether there was any joint manoeuvres with the JNA -- between the JNA and a neighbouring country, for instance. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will now address another topic which your counsel did not address. The question was mentioned several times. I would like to know what you think about the notion of All People's Defence. In your view, what does this mean, "All People's Defence"?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, at the time, when the political leadership of the then Yugoslavia considered that they had an enemy, an enemy mostly in the West, but it didn't believe its great friend in the East, either, didn't trust them too much, either, a theory was developed which allegedly gave good results through the Second World War, the theory of an armed people as a force to be reckoned with, a force that was invincible. And on that basis, the so-called concept of All People's Defence or Total National Defence was developed, so that everybody in the society had a role to play. Everybody had a war plan, everybody was part and parcel of this general effort and had tasks within the framework of the general plan of Total National Defence or All People's Defence. And Yugoslavia, in this way, wished to raise 5 to 6 million people able to resist what was called a total aggression, because nobody thought that Italy -- a country -- one country like Italy could attack Yugoslavia; it was backed by everything else, all the other states in which that country was an ally. Or if relations with the East deteriorated, no one thought that one eastern country would be alone in its appetites towards Yugoslavia but that it meant a whole bloc being the aggressor. So viewing the situation like that, they thought that the West was the principal foe, principal adversary, but reserving the right that not even a great friend from the East might always be a great friend. And so Yugoslavia was prepared for the worst possible situation, that it might be attacked by one or both blocs, according to spheres of interest, that something would then, if an attack came about, that something would come to belong to the East and something to the West. And I think that the Drina River was a sort of division between East and West, and that was the worst-case scenario which the leadership considered at the time; that is to say, that Yugoslavia might be attacked at one and the same time by both the Warsaw Pact and NATO, and that is why they devised this system of mass arming -- when I say "arming," I mean it quite literally, the mass arming of all structures of society. Let me just give you an example, the aluminium combine in Sibenik, for example. In the anti-air defence system, I think it had more resources and materiel than two brigades. Everything was bought by the workers, by setting aside a portion of their incomes. Or, for example, Zenica, the steelworks at Zenica had 10 tanks which belonged to the workers of the steelworks. They weren't new tanks, but they were either T-34 Russian tanks or the Shermans, or whatever. Nothing was thrown away. Everything was maintained and stored, and Yugoslavia was a real depot and warehouse. Look at what's happening in Albania. If something explodes in the north, there might be a detonation somewhere else or not. That was how they were linked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You explained a moment ago that in Yugoslavia, you were preparing against an attack of the Warsaw Pact or NATO. As you know, NATO at some point bombed Belgrade and its surroundings. You, as a former Yugoslav citizen turned Croat, what were your feelings about this?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't really know what my feelings were, how I felt in that respect. It was the first time -- now, although I was a long way away, it was the first time that I could follow what a war with NATO forces would look like; war at a distance, as we used to call it. He's destroying you, bombing you. Now, the way in which NATO attacked Yugoslavia, I do not accept. I do not accept that method. It is not acceptable, because the Chinese Embassy, Yes, you can destroy a television station, but at night, when there's no programme, the infrastructure being Novi Sad, whereas the front is 700 kilometres away in Kosovo. So your not confronting an army over there; you are choosing other targets. And then you say that a train was accidentally bombed and destroyed as it entered a certain region, and so on. So this was a war -- well, I also followed events in Iraq, but this was closer, closer to home. And then I saw that it was might and power that was being used in a too-uncontrolled way to inflict damage, damage to everything, but least of all to the army. And let me tell you when the Serb army, the JNA, withdrew from Kosovo, the Americans were surprised to see so many tanks, because they were firing somewhere, and columns of tanks were leaving Kosovo when there was a truce, and then they asked, Where are the ones that they destroyed? So it was a war to destroy the infrastructure and instill fear in the people and bring the people in a situation -- you know, if you keep cutting off electricity or use special means to destroy communication lines, or whatever, a long way from the front, and you don't have the courage to send in your land forces to clear up the area, then there's something -- well, regardless of the fact that NATO is a democratic army, wishing to instill a democratic order, I don't think that that's what they did in Serbia. However, they have a justification, which is accepted as such. Well, you see, that's it. That's the situation, and that's how I viewed it. If you lose one plane, you have 100 planes to find it and pull it out. The fact that hundreds of Serb ones were destroyed, never mind. So it was interesting to follow all this happening from a distance, and then you can engage in an analysis of the situation from a distance. So I was a bit surprised that that was the way a war was being conducted under new circumstances and conditions. Everything was done at a distance. Everything relied on technology. Everything was resolved by throwing -- not the army, but the people throwing to their knees. The Serb army, actually, didn't suffer too much. They didn't destroy any corps command, or brigade command, or anything like that. They didn't even send in their army. They tried to use their helicopters, but when they saw that they were being shot down, they didn't use them anymore either. To bring the people to their knees. So that's my view of the operation, and I really did think that it would happen along the front-lines. And, of course, if you happen to see a column along the way, it would be dealt with militarily. But to attack a structure of that kind in a country, I really couldn't have envisaged that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thanks to your answer, I can establish a connection with what General Praljak told us. He told us that while he exercised his command either as a volunteer or when he replaced you, he had been in contact with an American officer, whose name I will not mention. This American officer came on the spot on several occasions. As far as you know, when you were in command of the HVO, the Main Staff of the HVO, were you aware of the fact that there was an American presence, or did you know nothing about it, or was there no American presence? What can you tell me about that?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course there were some of their officers in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and they were led by one of our -- I think he was a Croat by origin, an NCO who was there and who went to Bosnia-Herzegovina. What? I can't hear what people are saying. But as an officer, well, I was with him a few times, but I can't remember his name now. I will remember by tomorrow. But, anyway, they went down there to size up the situation, and I assume that among the UNPROFOR people, there were those who were there, installed there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, have I made a mistake when I put my question? THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. I would just like to say this: General Petkovic says with that American -- well, there was a Croat with the American, so ask him whether that other one was an American soldier, wearing an American uniform as well, the man accompanying the American presence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, both of them were American soldiers. They were American soldiers. I just said that I knew one of these who knew Croatian, and he went around in Bosnia with them and around Croatia as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One point of detail which did not appear when General Praljak testified. These American officers, were they wearing an American uniform or were they in plain clothes?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, they wore American uniforms. I think they were navy blue in colour, with all the insignia and designation of rank and so on. And I thought that they were there quite legally. And they didn't hide from anybody, the ones I knew. They were there in full view. They would announce themselves, they would talk to us, so I assume -- well, they didn't want to uncover their true mission. They had a mission of some kind, but they moved around quite openly, wearing their uniforms and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to you, were they advisers or involved in the intelligence services?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were intelligence officers, first and foremost. They didn't advise anyone. They were desirous of information. And on one or two occasions with our man -- well, not "our man," but the man who was the Croat by origin, I met him three or four times, but they came to see what was happening and things like that. They did their work and acted quite properly. They protected what they were doing and that was their responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think I should say that in line 23 of the transcript, it would appear as if General Petkovic is saying that the Americans were intelligence officers, but in Croatian he used the word -- he said a sentence to this effect: that they most probably were. But you could ask him. That would be best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you did not know exactly, because my question was very clear. I was wondering whether they were military advisers, as we see them sometimes, or whether they were intelligence officers. I thought that they were doing intelligence work, but Mr. Kovacic said that you thought that they were rather doing that. So could you perhaps clarify?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said, Your Honours. An intelligence officer is not going to say, Listen here, Petkovic, I'm an intelligence officer and I'm going over there. So you have to assess this. Perhaps he wasn't. But these were people who were interested in many things. Now, whether he took a leave of absence, a month's holiday, to come to Bosnia-Herzegovina and put on an American uniform, I don't know. Whether he was an intelligence officer or not, I can't claim that either. He was an officer. They were officers and NCOs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So obviously they were not having a holiday there. But if I understand correctly, in 1992 and 1993 and 1994 there were, on the ground, the European Mission, UNPROFOR, journalists from the world press, as well as American officers. Am I forgetting anyone?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, there was the UNPROFOR, there was the European Observer Mission, there were the military observers who were independent and separate, there were representatives of the UNHCR, the International Red Cross Committee, and there were those who didn't provide a lot of assistance but wanted to see a whole lot of things, and they were the ones that collected up information and intelligence. And, you know, the governments of all the countries who were interested had, in a way, in addition to UNPROFOR and their forces there, to check out certain information in other ways, too, resort to other means.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We understood that some countries, who will remain nameless, had sent their agents there. I will come back to the Americans now. They were visible because they were wearing uniforms. When they were moving about, did they have some sort of an authorisation? What were they doing when they reached this check-point, or just the fact that they were wearing an American uniform allowed them to go anywhere in an easier way than displaying an American Express card?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, nobody stopped any groups like that or checked them. They would take a look at the uniform, saw that they were members of some armed force, and there were so many soldiers and army members in Bosnia, you could always say you belonged to SpaBat, or, BritBat, or the Canadian Battalion, the Nordic Battalion, or who knows which other ones, so if you -- if there were just two or three people in a vehicle, of course you would be let through. There was no problem in being let through, in passing through. They would say they were members of the international forces, and they would be let through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm coming now to a sensitive question. When the HVO launched a military operation, whichever that may be - I will not go into the details - I was wondering whether those American officers were aware, or whether you were doing that behind their back in order for them not to know, or was the situation such that you had nothing to hide and you knew that they would not shop you to the ABiH or to the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, as far as the operations were concerned, particularly offensive ones, we had nothing to show, because there were no operations on the scale that would be of interest to an American officer. Whether we would work within an area of 100 metres or not, that was it. So the representatives of the nearest UNPROFOR unit would go out into the field and see what was going on, and if they felt it was necessary to send out some more monitors, then they would go and control an area of, say, 60 kilometres, and then the European Observers would hear about this and they would get there, and then you had a whole array of international organisations, and finally you would see that the HVO had taken Feature 504, for example, or had lost control of Feature 708. But you would have six types of various international organisation representatives there, because each one of them had -- there was some shooting going on, and everybody wanted to report back first. So they would all find themselves on the spot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'm going to ask clearer questions or with more detail. I was wondering whether you personally spoke to those American officers or with other officers.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I talked to this one who was from Croatia originally. I think he was from Tomislavgrad, but left when he was a young man and joined the army. So I think I talked to him, but we didn't discuss anything special. He said, Well, we'd just like to come and see what's going on. We're just moving through, that's what he said. He wasn't very talkative and didn't say much. A man of few words. And that's the kind of people they were, because if you sent talkative people out, that wouldn't have been a good thing. The less you talked about what you were doing, the better, from their point of view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to look at the three events at stake here: The 9th of May, Sovici and Doljani in April, and the third event Stupni Do. I was wondering, as regards those three events, whether one of those officers would have said to you, face to face, General Petkovic, please explain to us what happened. Were you asked to give some sort of explanation? Because I assume that they had to report back to their relevant authorities, so I was wondering whether you had a position on that.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, you may not believe me, but here's what I have to say: They never came to the command to ask what was going on. When they did come, they -- it was as if nothing was going on anywhere. They have their own plan of work. On the 9th of May, I wasn't able to see or hear any one of them. Only on the 10th of May, in the evening, I think it was when I arrived at Kiseljak, there was General Prado - that was his name, I think - a Spaniard who was a member of the joint UNPROFOR command at Kiseljak, and I had a word with him. And I waited for Halilovic to come on the following day to have a meeting with him. Likewise, General Morillon, who contacted us more than anybody else, didn't tell such stories either, like, Now I'm going to draft an agreement, you're going to sign it, and then we'll implement it. They never interfered. They didn't ask questions, they didn't pass judgement. And to be honest, when I read a report the Spanish wrote, I was amazed at what I could read there. When it comes to Sovici and Doljani, and more generally the entire Konjic area, from the 13th of April on, they were unable to access the area. On the 8th of May, in Mostar, they requested the 4th Corps to finally let them enter that area. I found out about that later, because there were three ambassadors who had come to visit. They were blocked and couldn't enter those areas. General Pellnas tried to organise something like that, but was unsuccessful. I was there three or four times. There are documents containing my protests, et cetera. Although it was agreed otherwise, SpaBat would take me Kostajnica, and we would wait four hours and then we would return. I was only able to enter our church in Konjic. That's what I was able to reach. The furthest I could go was Kostajnica, but I was never able to go seven kilometres further to Klis. And I went to Ostrozac, where I had a very unpleasant conversation with SpaBat, because some of our people said, Protect us, we won't fight, there are over 100 civilians here. And then they handed over their rifles to the Spanish, but the Spanish, pressurized by Zuka and his people, delivered these 50 to 60 of our soldiers to Zuka. And I was -- I felt very uncomfortable. I was very struck by that. They could have protected them, because if the UNPROFOR makes a promise that they would do something, then they should have, even if it means using force. I even told them, Well, do use force once, and then such a situation will never reoccur. Let me tell you of an experience on the Road of Salvation. There was a BritBat. Probably two HVO soldiers were provoking them, but they lost their lives, because they opened fire at them. And then there was a discussion about that, and, well, we didn't want to make things worse. But I can tell you, later on nobody dared provoke them anymore. But you cannot say that a check-point, manned by three soldiers, can stop five APCs. Place a police car here on this road with five police officers, whoever is daring enough will break through with his car, and not to speak about five UNPROFOR APCs. But they would stop and speak for 10 or 20 minutes, and then make a report, Well, they stopped us at the check-point. But why did you stop? Because there's no way you can stop an APC there. An APC is armed with a machine-gun, and at the check-point there are three to five men with rifles, no more than that. And that was the suggestion I made to General Morillon. I told him, Come on, be more energetic in your conduct. But let me not go deeper into that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, certainly, you are addressing something which I hadn't contemplated. It is true that in a number of UNPROFOR reports, it appears that the HVO had established check-points. I'm saying "the HVO," but when I look at the military documents of the ABiH, I think the same would apply, so I am not establishing a selection here. At some of the HVO check-points, there were soldiers who were preventing UNPROFOR from passing. When I see that, I say to myself that they should have passed all the same because they are aboard APCs. Can you tell me whether UNPROFOR managed to get through or not? If they had managed to get through, would the HVO have fired at them?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you, Your Honours, anything could have happened. But let me give you the following example: The BritBat at Vitez. There was no stopping them with any check-points. When they start with four of their Warriors, Warrior vehicles, once they start moving, everybody would -- nobody would dare to try to stop them. And when the UNPROFOR came, they would stop and then engage in talks, Let me see who you are, et cetera. I took rides with the Spaniards like that. Riding with them to Kiseljak would have taken forever. But I also rode with the British. You know where they would stop. If the destination of our journey was Prozor, and that's the only place we stopped. And on the way there, they passed a number of check-points of both the HVO and the ABiH. It all depended on how they behaved. The commander of the BritBat said, Your commander signed that we have freedom of movement, and nobody is going to stop me. And that's how he went to Zenica and to Visoko, where the ABiH was, and that's the same way they moved between Visoko and Busovaca. That was the difference between them. Some of them were soft and waved sheets of paper about, which they weren't obliged to do, if it says "Freedom of Movement," and nobody had anti-armour weapons at those check-points because those check-points were meant for your own army and not for stopping the enemy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I've understood you correctly, because this is the first time -- even though the trial has been ongoing for four years, it's the first time that this issue is raised, you say that when, in the reports of the Spanish Bat, it is mentioned that the HVO was preventing people from passing, that's not quite what was happening, because if they'd wanted to, they could have gone through. What they usually did, they stopped off and talked to the people who were there, and then in the report they stated that they had been prevented from going through, whereas the British acted differently. They were on board their vehicles, they drove through, and there was no problem. That is what you're saying, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, exactly, Your Honour. He showed everybody that he had a warrant of freedom of movement, and nobody's going to stop him. And on the 29th of June, when they drove me, they weren't shot at by anybody. They said, We are not going to stop before we take the general to his destination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a shame that I hear about it so late. Had I known before, when the Spaniards came to testify here, I would have shown them their reports and I would have put the question to them directly. This is something I am discovering only now. Most importantly, it's on the transcript. So all this came from the American officers. As far as I'm concerned, it's all an open question. If you remember, Colonel Skender came here. He was a member of the French Foreign Legion, and he became an officer of the HVO. Ante Roso was also a member of the French Foreign Legion, if I remember correctly; so was Gotovina, and there must be a number of other people also. The fact that there was a Croatian presence there, people who had been officers in the French Army, was this just a question of chance or was it important to have men on the ground who had served in the French Army? I put the question to Colonel Skender. Remember, he came here to defend the Croats. But I didn't belabour the point. Since you were head of the Main Staff, you might have some idea.

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About Colonel Skender, I can only say that he told you the truth. When he came to Croatia, he didn't have any special tasks. He just wanted to join the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Initially, he really visited those people, advised them, because he wasn't a man who would sit around all day. He would move about. If you give him a vehicle, he would visit two brigades, talk to people, try to explain things to them. And then, whether it was in October 1993 or whenever, when he became commander, I don't know if Roso was a chief when Skender became commander, but, anyway, I believe that upon the request of General Roso, he agreed to take over the Command of the OZ South-West Herzegovina until somebody else can be found to replace him, and that's when he learned that it is one thing to be a person without a commanding duty, who is free to move about and advise people, and quite another thing when you're a commander, with all the responsibilities that go with that post. So I don't know how long he held out, how long he stayed in that position. As for General Roso, I was surprised by his -- by the fact that he agreed to take over that duty, because he had already been in the Croatian Army. I'm not sure what the brigade in the Croatian Army was called that Roso commanded. He also had a group of people of, I don't know, maybe up to 100 people, and Roso was also happy to move about from Slavonia to Dalmatia and Dubrovnik. He was also a guy who wouldn't stay put in one place. He was always with some special units, as they were called, and he had 20 or 30 of these from Osijek to Split and further on. And that's why I was surprised by the fact that Ante Roso came to join us down there, but otherwise I didn't object to that. He agreed to come and take over that duty. And as far as Gotovina is concerned, he was a non-commissioned officer in the French Army and became a high-ranking general in the HV, but Gotovina accepted to be the commander of the Operative Zone of Split. And he did a good job there because he was a capable man, but he also listened to his advisers. By the way, let me tell you, they weren't adventurers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, what I wanted to know is whether it was pure coincidence, the fact that all these people were there on the ground, or was it not a coincidence?

utterances.speaker: MILIVOJ PETKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't a coincidence. They weren't there by chance. We trusted those people, although they had previously commanded smaller units. Skender did have a high rank in the French Army, but the other two didn't. However, we thought that they had great wartime experience and that they would be very useful in working with those units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, we'll have to stop because we only have a few minutes left on the tape. If you're quick, please do -- THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] If I may, I would like to make a remark that there is a misunderstanding, because you asked a question quite some time ago, and your question was whether the Croats who were sending these people to the Foreign Legion because they wanted them to be prepared once they returned, or whether that was not the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that was the meaning of my question. General Petkovic, you have answered the questions. We will have to stop now. The tapes have run out. It's 6.00. On Monday -- well, this was a starter. I shall discuss the main dish on Monday and discuss your role as indicated in the indictment and the JCE. Then we will look into the documents. You have a few days to prepare for this. I wish everyone a pleasant evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
